blocks.text: In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

The Arabic letter bāʾ at the start of the basmalah can express seeking help or being accompanied. When a servant begins reciting in Allah’s name, they seek His help and hope that the blessing of His name will accompany them throughout their recitation. The same applies to their journey to Allah. They need His help from the beginning and at every step, before they run out of other means. The Prophet ﷺ expressed this need in a supplication for someone in distress: “O Allah! Thy mercy is what I hope for. Do not abandon me to myself for an instant.”

The opening brings together the two names “the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.” They teach the heart to know its Lord through His mercy, so the servant approaches the Qur’an and goes through life seeking His help and mercy in matters great and small. The servant has not simply chosen the names they most like to mention. Allah Himself taught His servants to remember these names in this opening. We come to know Him through what He has revealed about Himself. When the worshipper is mindful of these meanings, recitation becomes a conscious act of seeking help and hoping in Him, with words the heart understands as the tongue says them.

blocks.text: All praise be to Allah[1], the Lord[2] of the worlds[3],

To praise Allah is to extol Him with love and submission. Its scope is wider than gratitude for a particular blessing. A person may thank their Lord when they get what they hoped for and, if deprived of it, feel no inclination to praise Him. Yet Allah deserves praise for the perfection of His names and attributes, the beauty of His creation, and the greatness of His blessings, whether or not the person gets what they hoped for. True praise comes from knowing Allah in a way that fills the heart with love and reverence for Him. It goes beyond naming His beautiful attributes. The Arabic definite article al- in al-ḥamd, “praise,” encompasses every kind of praise. All praise belongs to Allah, whether a person recognizes its reasons or cannot see them.

Al-Aswad ibn Sarīʿ came to the Prophet ﷺ and told him he had prepared words in praise of his Lord. The Prophet ﷺ said, “Your Lord loves praise.” One of the honors bestowed on the Prophet ﷺ is that he will hold the Banner of Praise on the Day of Resurrection. When he prostrates before Allah at the station of intercession, Allah will teach him words of praise and beautiful commendation that He taught no one before him. This invites us to consider what we praise Allah for and to praise Him in varied ways, glorifying Him, thanking Him for His blessings, and contemplating the greatness of His creation. We can say “all praise be to Allah” with its meaning in mind, beyond the force of habit.

We may overlook the value of the blessings we live with each day. Seeing people who are ill helps us appreciate well-being. Seeing those who have strayed from Allah’s path helps us appreciate guidance. In good health, our bodies carry out many functions without our noticing or having to direct them. We may only appreciate some of them when we fall ill or see someone suffering from their loss. The more carefully we consider the details of what Allah has given us, the more we recognize His favor and feel the need to thank Him. We need not wait until a blessing is gone to recognize its worth.

A person may become so occupied with a hardship that they overlook Allah’s blessings. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī explained Allah’s words “indeed, man is very ungrateful to his Lord[5]” [Al-ʿĀdiyāt 100:6] by saying that he counts his troubles and forgets his blessings. We may be able to list our problems one by one while remaining unable to count what Allah has given us. Allah says, “If you try to count the blessings of Allah, you cannot count them[25]” [Ibrāhīm 14:34]. A person may still grieve over what has happened and ask Allah to lift the hardship. The point is to remember His other blessings even amid the hardship.

At the opening of Al-Kahf, the servant praises Allah for revelation: “All praise be to Allah Who has sent down upon His slave the Book” [Al-Kahf 18:1]. In Al-Fatihah, the servant praises Allah because this universe has a Lord who sustains it, directs its affairs, and has given it purpose. This lordship includes both ownership of creation and nurturing creatures with what they need at each stage of life. A child takes shape in its mother’s womb, as Allah says, “He creates you in the wombs of your mothers [in stages], creation after creation, in three layers of darkness[6]” [Az-Zumar 39:6]. A seed is placed in the soil, a root reaches toward water, and then the stem, leaves, and fruit emerge as the plant grows.

The effects of this lordship can be seen in each creature’s growth and in how creatures are connected and depend on one another. A plant grows and produces fruit suited to nourishing a person. An animal feeds on plants and grows, and people benefit from its meat. Allah has provided the human body with what it needs to digest food and distribute nourishment to its organs. Every stage depends on Allah’s ordering. The same applies to the sun’s course, the earth’s movement, the falling of rain, and every breath we take and every beat of the heart.

The discoveries scientists make about the grandeur of the universe can fill a person with wonder, as when the image of a black hole appeared. That wonder should lead them to glorify the One who created the universe and set its order with precision. Allah says, “We built the heaven with might[13], and We are indeed expanding it.” [Adh-Dhāriyāt 51:47] He also says, “Are the disbelievers not aware that the heavens and earth were joined together and then We split them apart?” [Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:30] Allah did not create the universe and then leave it to stand on its own. It continues through His governance. “Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep[145]” [Al-Baqarah 2:255]. When the servant says “the Lord[2] of the worlds[3],” they bring to mind the worlds of human beings, jinn, angels, animals, and plants, and their many branches, down to creatures too small to see with the naked eye.

Some scholars have noted a connection between the Arabic word ʿālam, “world,” and ʿalāmah, “sign.” Each of these worlds, with its creatures and precise order, points to its Creator. When a person considers how all these creatures need Allah at every moment, they begin to grasp the meaning of “All praise be to Allah[1], the Lord[2] of the worlds[3].” One of Allah’s great favors is that He answers His servant when the servant praises Him with these words. In the sacred hadith, Allah says, “I have divided the prayer into two halves between Me and My servant, and My servant will receive what he asks.” When the servant says “All praise be to Allah[1], the Lord[2] of the worlds[3],” Allah says, “My servant has praised Me.” [Muslim 395]

In this hadith, Allah calls Al-Fatihah “the prayer” because of its great place within prayer. Likewise, the Prophet ﷺ said, “The Hajj is Arafah.” [At-Tirmidhi 889] Hajj has several rites, but it is invalid without standing at ʿArafah. Al-Fatihah likewise holds a great place in prayer. One way to recite it with humble attention is to remember that we are speaking privately to our Lord, who hears and answers us. When we say “All praise be to Allah[1], the Lord[2] of the worlds[3],” Allah answers, “My servant has praised Me.” Remembering this exchange helps us reflect on what Allah has given us, so the heart praises Him along with the tongue.

ʿUrwah ibn Az-Zubayr asked ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both) for his daughter’s hand while they were circling the Kaʿbah. Ibn ʿUmar did not answer at the time. When they later met in Madinah, he explained that he had been deeply conscious of standing before Allah while performing ṭawāf. He then gave his daughter in marriage to him. Speaking during ṭawāf is permitted, as Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) indicated when he likened it to prayer but allowed speaking during it. Yet Ibn ʿUmar was so occupied with remembering Allah’s greatness that he put aside a conversation of such importance. What, then, of prayer, in which talking to other people is impermissible and about which the Prophet ﷺ said, “In the prayer one is occupied (with a more serious matter).” [Al-Bukhari 1199, Muslim 538] In prayer we praise and extol Allah, speak to Him privately, and ask Him for what we need. These acts give the heart enough to attend to without turning to the worldly matters waiting afterward.

The order of the verses in Al-Fatihah teaches us how to ask. When a person approaches someone who can grant an important request, they take care with how they present it. They begin with a greeting and praise, then say who they are and explain their need before making the request. To Allah belongs the highest example. Allah taught His servants how to ask for their greatest need, guidance. The opening verses praise and glorify Allah. Then, by saying “You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help,” the servant acknowledges being Allah’s servant and needing His help. Only then comes the request repeated in every unit of prayer, “Guide us to the straight path.” So great is this request that Allah Himself taught the servant the words for asking Him for guidance. He did not leave the wording for the servant to choose.

quranNotes.text:
[1] Allah is God’s most unique name.
 [2] The Arabic term "rabb" (translated as "Lord") includes all of the following meanings: "owner, master, ruler, controller, sustainer, provider, guardian and caretaker."
 [3] "the worlds" means mankind, jinn, and all that exists.
[5] disobeying Him by not spending in the cause of Allah from what He has given him and commanded him to spend accordingly.

[24] It is not only these grand favors that Allah grants people, but their prayers are also answered, be they uttered or merely wished for.
 [25] If a person were to ever try to count Allah’s blessings on him, he would never be able to count them, let alone be duly grateful for them.

[3] i.e., Adam. [4] i.e., Eve. [5] The eight types of livestock: (four males and females): a pair of sheep, a pair of goats, a pair of camels, and a pair of oxen. See 6:143-144.
 [6] These three layers: the belly, the womb, and the amniotic membrane.
[13] ’Ayd does not mean "hands" here. This is not from the verses of Allah's attributes, for Allah Almighty did not add it to Himself, i.e., He did not say, "My ’ayd, or Our ’ayd".

[143] Whose life is perfect, complete, and eternal, without beginning or end.
 [144] Dependent on none for His existence while being the sustainer of all created beings.
 [145] Dozing off and falling asleep are but normal to all creation that are inherently frail.
 [146] Allah's knowledge encompasses every aspect of His creations in the past, present and future.
 [147] Chair or footstool. It is not to be confused with al-‘Arsh (the Throne), which is infinitely higher and greater than al-Kursī.
 [148] Above all of His creations and superior to them in essence, rank, and position.
 [149] Whose greatness is unlimited, beyond description or imagination.
 [150] This verse is known as Āyat al-Kursī, lit. The verse of the Footstool. It is the greatest verse in the Qur’an.

blocks.text: the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful[4],

After the servant reflects on the greatness of Allah’s creation, His power, and His ordering of the worlds, they hear of His mercy before hearing of the Day of Reckoning. They know then that they are going to a merciful Lord and hope to reach the Day of Judgment safe and at peace. In the sacred hadith, when the servant says “the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful[4],” Allah says, “My servant has lauded Me.”

One explanation of the difference between the names is that Ar-Raḥmān points to Allah’s vast, immense mercy, while Ar-Raḥīm points to His mercy reaching the servant in the smallest details of life. Sūrat Maryam gives examples of the breadth of that mercy. It repeatedly mentions Ar-Raḥmān and recounts great miracles, including the gift of Yaḥyā to Zakariyyā, peace be upon him, in his old age and the birth of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, without a father. Some scholars have said that placing Ar-Raḥīm after Ar-Raḥmān reminds the servant to ask for Allah’s help in the affairs of their home, children, and work, even in something as small as mending a sandal, as well as in great matters. This explanation describes a mercy so vast that it embraces the smallest details of human life without dividing it into two separate kinds.

Another effect of Allah’s mercy and forbearance is that He does not hasten to bring about every harm people call down upon themselves or their families in anger. Allah says, “If Allah were to hasten evil[14] to the people, just as they seek to hasten good[15], they would have been ruined.” [Yūnus 10:11] He also shows mercy by not hastening to punish His servants for every sin. “If Allah were to take people to task for what they did, He would not leave a single living being on earth, but He gives them respite for an appointed term.” [Fāṭir 35:45] This respite is an opportunity to repent and return to Allah, while the sin remains liable to punishment.
Allah gives His servants time and opens the doors of repentance and return to them. The Prophet ﷺ told us that our Lord descends to the lowest heaven when the last third of the night remains and calls on His servants to supplicate, ask, and seek forgiveness. The Prophet ﷺ also said, “Verily, Allah Almighty extends His Hand during the night so the sinner of the day may repent, and He extends His Hand during the day so the sinner of the night may repent.” A servant should never let the length of time they have turned away from Allah lead them to despair of His mercy or keep sinning.

The Prophet ﷺ told us that Allah rejoices more at His servant’s repentance than a man rejoices when he recovers his mount in the desert. The man had lost his mount, with his food and drink on it, and had given up hope of finding it or surviving before he found it again. Imagine a person’s joy when the means of staying alive come back to them. Allah rejoices even more when His servant turns to Him in repentance. In the sacred hadith, Allah says, “My Mercy overpowers My Anger.” [Al-Bukhari 3194]

Knowing how vast Allah’s mercy is should shape how the servant calls people to Him and treats them. As we hope Allah will show us mercy and overlook our shortcomings, we should treat people with mercy, remind them how vast His mercy is, and help them repent without making their sin seem trivial or driving them to despair of His forgiveness.

quranNotes.text: [4] Ar-Rahmān and Ar-Raheem are two names of Allah: Rahmān is used only to describe Allah, while raheem might be used to describe a human as well. Rahmān carries a wider meaning - merciful to all creation. Justice is a part of this mercy. Raheem includes the concept of specialty - especially merciful to the believers. Forgiveness is a part of this mercy. In addition, Rahmān is adjectival, referring to an attribute of Allah and is part of His essence. Raheem is verbal, indicating what He does: i.e., bestowing and implementing mercy.

[14] i.e., invoking against oneself or one’s children in anger.
 [15] “Man prays for evil as he prays for good, for man is ever hasty.” See 17:11.

blocks.text: Master[5] of the Day of Judgment.

The Day of Judgment is the day of reckoning and recompense. People will submit to Allah’s judgment and be repaid for their deeds. One point to reflect on in the choice of this name is that the Arabic word dīn also refers to the way Allah commanded people to follow in this life. The two meanings are connected. Allah calls people to account according to the truth He made clear to them and the law He revealed. Believing in the Day of Judgment therefore affects the choices we make now. We may find a decision difficult when we consider only its immediate consequences. Thinking of its consequences in the Hereafter changes how we weigh it. Allah described believers with the words “and in the Hereafter they believe with certainty” [Al-Baqarah 2:4]. He also showed what turns a person away from the truth: “No indeed! You [people] love this fleeting world, and neglect the Hereafter.” [Al-Qiyāmah 75:20–21]

Two mass-transmitted readings have come down to us, ﴿مَالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ﴾ and ﴿مَلِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ﴾. The first uses mālik, the word for master or owner, and the second uses malik, the word for king. Allah owns that day, including its judgment and recompense, and He is the King whose authority no one can dispute. He owns and rules this world and the Hereafter. The Day of Judgment is named here because people in this life may be deluded by the authority and strength Allah has given them and use it to act arrogantly and wrong others. Pharaoh said, “I am your lord, the most high.” [An-Nāziʿāt 79:24] The people of ʿĀd said, “Who is more powerful than us?” [Fuṣṣilat 41:15] Allah drowned Pharaoh and destroyed ʿĀd with the wind. The power and authority that had deluded them disappeared.

Allah reminds us of what became of earlier peoples: “Do you sense a single one of them or even hear from them a whisper?” [Maryam 19:98] Can you perceive anyone among them or hear even a faint sound? They once filled the world with their voices and claims. Now none of them remains. On the Day of Resurrection it will be clear to all creation that dominion belongs to Allah alone. “To whom does the dominion belong this Day[4]? To Allah, the One, the Subjugator!” [Ghāfir 40:16] And creation will submit to Him. “All faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, Self-Sustaining” [Ṭā Hā 20:111]. No one will speak except with His permission.

The Prophet ﷺ told us that people will be gathered barefoot and naked [Al-Bukhari 6527, Muslim 2859]. The sun will draw close to them that day, and their sweat will reach different levels according to their deeds [Muslim 2864]. A person who lived in a palace and could secure comfort and protection through money and authority will stand on that day having lost all they possessed. Their standing among people will offer no protection from the terrors of the day. People’s circumstances will differ according to their deeds.

The hadith tells us that the arrogant will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection “resembling tiny particles in the image of men,” with humiliation enveloping them from every side. Those who acted arrogantly toward others because of their wealth or power will come that day utterly small and humiliated. Bringing this scene to mind helps us avoid being deluded by what Allah has given us in this life and remember that we are His servants, whatever our standing among people.

The words “Master[5] of the Day of Judgment” follow “the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful[4]” and answer many questions raised by the suffering and injustice we see. When a child suffers because of war or a victim is tortured and finds no one to do them justice, someone may ask how these things can happen when Allah is compassionate and merciful. This world is a place of trials, and a person’s life does not end here. Allah says, “if Allah had willed, He could have subjected them to punishment, but [He ordered you to fight] to test some of you by means of others” [Muḥammad 47:4]. Delaying punishment for a wrongdoer does not suggest that Allah is unable to punish them or unaware of what they do. Allah says, “Never think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do[29]; He only delays them for a Day when eyes will stare [in horror][30]” [Ibrāhīm 14:42].

If life ended with this world, both the murderer and the one they killed would die, as would both the oppressor and their victim, without the wronged person fully recovering their right from the one who wronged them. Allah has appointed a day of reckoning. His justice will be manifest then, wrongs will be redressed, and those who did good will be rewarded for it. Allah says, “We will place the scales of justice on the Day of Resurrection, and no soul will be wronged in the least. Even if a deed is the weight of a mustard seed[18], We will bring it forth. Sufficient are We as Reckoners.” [Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:47] In Sūrat Al-Muṭaffifīn, Allah describes the believers whom the evildoers mocked in this life. The scene is reversed in the Hereafter. They are described in the words “while sitting on couches, gazing around” [Al-Muṭaffifīn 83:35].

In the sacred hadith, when the servant says “Master[5] of the Day of Judgment,” Allah says, “My servant has glorified Me.” Another wording is, “My servant entrusted (his affairs) to Me.” One implication is that a wronged person can trust Allah’s justice and know that their right will not be lost with Him, even if they cannot recover it in this world. This is no invitation to accept injustice or give up trying to end it. A person who has wronged others and remembers the Day of Judgment will fear that it may come before they have restored people’s rights and repented of the wrong.

As we take care to prepare our children for their future in this life, we should also teach them to remember the Day of Judgment, when they will be called to account for what they say and do. The Prophet ﷺ said, “Indeed a man may utter a statement that he does not see any harm in, but for which he will fall seventy autumns in the Fire.” Someone may regard a word as trivial and fail to grasp its seriousness in the scales of the Hereafter. A servant who remembers that they will stand before Allah and answer for what they have done will return people’s rights without delay and will not let hoped-for worldly comforts lead them to neglect their religion.

quranNotes.text: [5] Other meanings for "Mālik": Sovereign, Owner, etc.

[4] According to a long narration known as the Trumpet Hadith, whose chain is weak, when all creatures have perished and none remains but Allah, He will ask, “To whom does the dominion belong this Day?” Since no one will be there to answer, He will answer Himself, “To Allah, the One, the Subjugator!” It is authentically reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: “Allah will seize the earth and fold up the heavens in His Right Hand, then He will say, ‘I am the King; where are the kings of the earth?’” [Sahih al-Bukhāri: 4812; Sahih Muslim: 2787]

[4] Ar-Rahmān and Ar-Raheem are two names of Allah: Rahmān is used only to describe Allah, while raheem might be used to describe a human as well. Rahmān carries a wider meaning - merciful to all creation. Justice is a part of this mercy. Raheem includes the concept of specialty - especially merciful to the believers. Forgiveness is a part of this mercy. In addition, Rahmān is adjectival, referring to an attribute of Allah and is part of His essence. Raheem is verbal, indicating what He does: i.e., bestowing and implementing mercy.

[29] It serves both as comfort to the oppressed and as a warning to the oppressors.
 [30] Because of the horrifying sights they see, they will be unblinkingly staring upwards in horror.
[18] i.e., as small or insignificant as a mustard seed.

blocks.text: You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.

After praising Allah and recalling His mercy and His dominion on the Day of Judgment, the servant moves from speaking about the Lord to speaking directly to Him. The servant does not say, “We worship Him and ask Him for help,” but says, “You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.” Scholars of Arabic rhetoric call this shift from the third person to direct address iltifāt.

One way to reflect on this shift is to consider what happens as the servant ponders Allah’s blessings, remembers the breadth of His mercy and the greatness of His dominion, and recalls standing before Him on the Day of Resurrection. Faith and reverence grow, and the servant draws nearer to Allah until they speak to Him as though they see Him. This is the station of iḥsān that the Prophet ﷺ explained in these words: “It is to worship Allah as if you see Him, for if you do not see Him, He sees you.” [Muslim 8] The verses before “You alone we worship” prepare the heart to speak to Allah in this way, with the greatness of the One being addressed present in mind.

The servant does not simply say naʿbuduka, “we worship You.” In “You alone we worship,” the word iyyāka, “You,” comes first to show that Allah alone is worshipped. A person may acknowledge Allah as their Creator and Provider, yet affirming His oneness requires worshipping Him alone. The Prophet’s supplication is fitting here: “O Allah, I am Your slave, and the son of Your male slave, and the son of your female slave.” [Aḥmad 3712] Before asking for what they need, the servant acknowledges who they are. Their servitude to Allah is their enduring condition and that of the fathers and mothers who came before them.

Worship brings together love of Allah and submission to Him. It includes outward acts and what is in the heart of love for Allah, reverence for Him, and acceptance of His command. The Arabic word for worship also carries the sense of being made submissive or yielding. The Arabs call a road muʿabbad when it has been smoothed and made easy to travel.

Submission to Allah extends beyond the times of ritual worship into every area of life. Its sincerity becomes clear when Allah’s command goes against what the self desires or what people expect. Whoever lives by “You alone we worship” seeks to align their desires with what Allah has prescribed, without seeking to change His ruling to fit their desires or putting other people’s approval ahead of their Lord’s. The Prophet ﷺ said, “There is no obedience in disobedience to Allah. Obedience is only in what is right.” [Muslim 1840] A person may grow so attached to money that acquiring it matters more to them than obeying Allah. The Prophet ﷺ warned, “Wretched is the servant of the dinar and the servant of the dirham.” [Al-Bukhari 2887]

A person may sincerely want to obey Allah and still give in under pressure from the people around them. Society can influence someone to see as good what human nature recoils from, as happened to some idolaters when killing their children was made to seem appealing. Allah says, “Similarly, the [evil] associates of the pagans have made the killing of their children[45] appealing to many of them” [Al-Anʿām 6:137]. A person may find themselves among people accustomed to backbiting or taking bribes and find it hard to go against them despite knowing that what they are doing is forbidden. The servant therefore asks Allah for help to obey Him and persevere, without relying on willpower alone. After “You alone we worship” comes “and You alone we ask for help.”

The two verbs naʿbudu (“we worship”) and nastaʿīnu (“we ask for help”) are plural. The servant does not say, in the singular, “I worship You alone and ask You alone for help.” By reciting Al-Fatihah, they bring to mind the worship of all believers and hope Allah will join them to His righteous servants despite their shortcomings. On the journey to Allah, they need good companions who help them obey Him and remain steadfast. Seeking people’s help with things within their ability is compatible with depending on Allah alone, as long as the servant knows that Allah made these means available and enabled them to benefit from them.

The servant can only fulfill their aim of worshipping Allah with His help. The Prophet ﷺ said in his supplication, “My (power as well as existence) is due to Thee (Thine grace) and I turn to Thee (for supplication).” [Muslim 771] The servant seeks Allah’s help in what they do and directs their intention toward Him. One of Allah’s great favors is that He helps the servant obey Him and then rewards them for it. In dealing with people, an employer might be surprised if an applicant asked the employer to help them do the very work they would be paid for. To Allah belongs the highest example. Allah enables His servant to obey Him, then rewards them for what He helped them do and admits them to Paradise by His grace and mercy.

When the servant realizes that Allah is the One who enables obedience, their heart will not become dependent on the means that help them obey. They may be moved by a Qur’an reciter’s beautiful voice or benefit from a teacher’s explanation or from reading a book. They may benefit from these means at one time and feel no effect from them at another. The servant should keep asking Allah for guidance. In the sacred hadith, Allah says, “O My servants, all of you are astray except for those I have guided, so seek guidance of Me and I shall guide you” [Muslim 2577].

When the servant recites “You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help,” Allah says, as reported in the sacred hadith, “This is between Me and My servant, and My servant will receive what he asks for.” [Muslim 395] The servant first mentions what Allah wants of them, worship, and then what they hope to receive from Him, help in worshipping Him. One reflection on “This is between Me and My servant” is that Allah alone knows how sincerely someone wishes to obey Him and how deeply they recognize their need for Him.

The effect of this sincere desire can be seen in the servant’s eagerness to learn what Allah loves and to do it. When they learn that the Prophet ﷺ said, “Two expressions are beloved to the Most Compassionate, easy on the tongue, and heavy on the Scale: Subḥān Allāhi wa bi-ḥamdih, Subḥān Allāhi l-ʿAẓīm,” [Al-Bukhari 7563] they are eager to repeat them out of love for what Allah loves. Knowing the different levels of rulings and distinguishing obligatory acts from recommended ones is important. A servant seeking Allah’s pleasure also strives to do whatever they can of the acts of obedience He loves, beyond what it would be sinful to omit.

Mosques may fill with worshippers for Friday prayer, while fewer people attend the afternoon prayer on the same day. Yet in both cases the caller says, “Come to prayer.” This is an invitation to examine our reasons for obeying Allah and how eager we are to do so when fewer people around us are doing the same.

The more sincerely a servant desires to worship Allah and asks for His help, the more this can lead to Allah granting them guidance. That is why, after acknowledging their servitude and their need for help, they make the greatest request they need to put to their Lord: “Guide us to the straight path.”

blocks.text: Guide us to the straight path,

Guidance is the great request Allah taught us to repeat in every unit of prayer. Al-Fatihah is thus repeated in the seventeen units of the obligatory prayers over a day and night when those prayers are performed in full. If a person were left to choose what to ask for in each unit, they might choose one of the worldly needs occupying them. Allah knows best what His servant needs. He knows the servant’s weakness in the face of desires and doubts and how many things can turn them away from the truth. He therefore chose for the servant to ask for guidance.

A person can take care of their worldly needs while keeping them in perspective. The Prophet ﷺ prayed, “do not make this world our greatest concern.” He did not ask that it be none of our concerns. It is natural to care about one’s livelihood, family, and health. Preserving one’s religion should matter more. The Prophet ﷺ said, “Ask Allah for pardon and Al-`Āfiyah (well-being). None of you is given anything after Yaqeen (certainty), anything better than Al-`Āfiyah (well-being).” Well-being is a great blessing that people seek. The blessing of certainty is greater.

The person who says “Guide us to the straight path” is already standing before Allah in prayer. They still ask for guidance because they fear losing what Allah has granted them and hope to grow in it. If what they already know of faith has brought them ease and improved their condition, what of the meanings they have yet to discover? A Muslim should welcome someone’s prayer for their guidance without taking it as an accusation of falling short. However righteous a person becomes, they still need to remain steadfast and grow in guidance.

One meaning of guidance is to show the way and lead someone gently. When the servant says “Guide us to the straight path,” they ask Allah to show them the path of truth and help them travel it. One reflection on the wording ﴿اهدنا الصراط﴾ is that this asks for guidance at every stage of the path, as well as at its beginning. The straight path begins with faith in Allah. A person proceeds along it by following His law and worshipping Him. Its destination lies beyond the end of this life, as the servant hopes it will lead to Paradise.

As a person advances along this path, they meet new temptations and situations they have never faced before. They may become deluded by their knowledge and worship and believe that they could never stray after recognizing the truth. Then they may fall into self-admiration, be overcome by a desire, or be misled by a doubt. Allah says, “And relate to them [O Prophet] the story of the one[72] whom We gave knowledge of Our revelations, but he abandoned it, so Satan took hold of him and he became one of the deviants.” [Al-Aʿrāf 7:175] Here was a man to whom Allah gave His signs, who then abandoned them. Even Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, a leader in worshipping Allah alone, prayed to his Lord, “and save me and my children from worshiping idols” [Ibrāhīm 14:35].

The Prophet ﷺ said, “Temptations will be presented to men's hearts as reed mat is woven stick by stick.” Trials keep coming to the heart. Having overcome one in the past offers no guarantee against the next. What someone sees or hears online may open the door to doubts and desires when they lack the knowledge to answer those doubts or the strength of faith to resist those desires. People who know the value of guidance will take care to guard it, just as they would guard a precious possession they fear losing.

Even when a person fears losing guidance, falling into sin should never make them despair of Allah’s mercy. They may disobey Allah between one prayer and the next, then stand for the next prayer and ask again for guidance, working to repair what they have damaged. The morning prayer of ḍuḥā, prayer at night, and other voluntary prayers offer further chances to renew this request. Each time the servant stumbles on the way to Allah, they need to get back up. Their failings should never lead them to give in or think that they have fallen short too often to become upright.

The servant’s hope extends beyond this life. They hope to come to the Prophet’s ﷺ pool and to cross safely over the bridge laid across Hell. The Prophet ﷺ told us that believers will cross it at different speeds. Some will cross in the blink of an eye, some like lightning or the wind, birds, or the swiftest horses and camels. Some will pass unharmed, some will cross after being scratched, and some will fall into the Fire. Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, may Allah be pleased with him, said, “I have come to know that the bridge would be thinner even than the hair and sharper than the sword.”

One way to reflect on the straight path is to remember how remaining upright in this life is connected to the deliverance one hopes for in the Hereafter. The servant asks Allah to keep them firm on the path of truth until they reach its destination. Others have already walked this path. The next verse tells the servant about those who went before, whom Allah blessed with guidance.

quranNotes.text: [72] A man from the Children of Israel at the time of Moses.

reportCredits: Sahih Muslim 183b; Abu Said report, not direct Prophetic attribution · Sunnah.com

blocks.text: the path of those whom You have blessed[6]; not of those who incurred Your Wrath[7], or of those who went astray[8].

When the servant says “the path of those whom You have blessed[6],” they ask Allah to join them to those who went before them on this road. They bring to mind the prophets, foremost among them our Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ, then his Companions among the emigrants and the helpers, and those who followed them with excellence. These people lived by the meanings of this religion and put them into practice. We should therefore know that the uprightness we ask for is possible and that our time is still a time to live by this religion. The Prophet ﷺ said, “A group from my community will continue to prevail on the path of truth. Those who desert them will not harm them until Allah’s command comes, and they will still be in that state.”

Among the words that give the servant hope of joining those guided before them are Allah’s words, “And [he is also sent] to others of them who have not yet joined them” [Al-Jumuʿah 62:3]. The servant reflects on the words “those whom You have blessed[6]”. With all the work and effort those people made, they could not have followed this path without Allah guiding them and helping them obey Him. The servant asks their Lord for the same blessing. Allah praised those who made the Pledge of His Pleasure: “Allah was much pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you [O Prophet] under the tree. He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down tranquility upon them” [Al-Fatḥ 48:18]. The servant is asking Allah to let them live by the guidance of people with whom He was pleased.

A man asked the Prophet ﷺ about someone who loved a people but had not attained their level. The Prophet ﷺ replied, “Everyone will be with those whom he loves.” This gives hope to a person who loves the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions even if they have not reached their level in knowledge and deeds. That love urges the servant to follow their example. They ask Allah for guidance that goes beyond identifying as Muslim, seeking His help to follow the Sunnah of His Prophet ﷺ and stay firm on his guidance.

Just as the servant asks the Lord to join them to those He has blessed, they ask Him to keep them away from the path of those who incurred His anger and those who went astray. In the report of ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, may Allah be pleased with him, the Prophet ﷺ explained that the Jews are among those who incurred anger and the Christians are among those who went astray. One way to incur anger is to know the truth and insist on acting against it. One way to go astray is to act without sound knowledge and follow one’s desires instead of receiving guidance. Uprightness requires both knowing the truth and acting on it. A Muslim should never assume that calling themselves Muslim makes them immune to either failing. They may know Allah’s ruling in a matter and go against it to satisfy a desire, or worship Allah without knowledge.

One effect of this supplication is to make us attentive, when reading the Qur’an, to the deeds that Allah says bring His anger upon those who do them or deprive them of His purification, and to the deeds that lead to error and misery. We can examine ourselves and take care to avoid such actions. The supplication also shapes our choice of example. A person who asks Allah to live by the guidance of the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions should avoid making ideas and values that run against their guidance the basis of their religion and way of life merely because they admire the people who hold them or the success they have achieved.

The close of Al-Fatihah brings hope and fear together. The servant hopes Allah will join them to those He has blessed and fears that pride, a desire, or a doubt might turn them from the path. Having guidance today gives no guarantee of remaining firm upon it to the end of life. That is why the servant repeats this request in every unit of prayer. Another source of hope is the sacred hadith in which Allah says, after this request, “This is for My servant, and My servant will receive what he asks for.” [Muslim 395]

The servant concludes by saying āmīn, meaning “O Allah, answer this prayer.” Āmīn is itself a supplication and lies outside the verses of Al-Fatihah. The servant says it with the greatness of what they have asked for in mind, hoping Allah will answer. By Allah’s grace, the angels say āmīn to this supplication too. The Prophet ﷺ said, “When the Imām says amen, you too say amen, for whoever says amen at the same time the angels say amen will have his previous sins forgiven.” [Al-Bukhari 780, Muslim 410]

In this short surah, Allah has brought together the foundations of meanings He explains in the rest of the Qur’an. When the servant reads verses about Allah’s attributes, names, and blessings, they gain a greater knowledge of the One they praise in Al-Fatihah. When they read verses about the Last Day, they deepen their understanding of “Master[5] of the Day of Judgment.” In the accounts of the prophets and righteous people, they recognize the qualities of those Allah has blessed and how they travelled the path to guidance. In the accounts of those who incurred anger and those who went astray, they recognize the deeds and traits they need to guard against to stay on the path. As their understanding of the Qur’an grows, they return to Al-Fatihah in prayer with a deeper understanding of what they say privately to their Lord and ask of Him.
